**TL;DR:** if two things are different in 99 aspects and only similar in 1, they should be two different types IMO.

**Long reply:**
I have a couple of issues with the proposed approach. First of all, I can't really see any benefit in having 1 subscribe method with 1 abstraction as topic/event def. Why is it really the requirement? 

On the contrary, I see several disadvantages here:
> our pubsub impl publisher can throw if you ever try to publish to a channel that's not Pub/Sub + source == current project

And it is exactly what I don't like here. Because we are trying to design in a way that we have "convenient subscribe" (which again is questionable in my opinion, more on that later), we actually have to replace compile time safety with runtime errors in case we try to mistakenly publish to what is currently named `EventDef`. Also `PubsubMessagingChannel` with `source == MessagingSource.GOOGLE` is a very different thing from `PubsubMessagingChannel` with `source == MessagingSource.IRIS`, because again you shouldn't be able to publish in the former. Why do they share the same type though? 

> subscribe would just take `MessagingChannel<T>` and `Consumer<T>`

Why exactly is this any good? 
1. Implementation is still different, right? So you gonna have type checks in `PubSubImpl` anyway, and two different methods anyway.
2. Okay, maybe because you will be then able to pass `List<MessagingChannel>` somewhere as method / constructor argument which can include both event channels and pubsub channels, right? Well... then you will be in more trouble and you will need to be even more aware of what is the type hierarchy there. Because you still need to differentiate between those types to avoid `RuntimeException`s and do type checks, casts, whatever so that you don't accidentally try to create a producer for `EventarcChannel`. 

Have a look at `nutshell.shared.polyflow.PolyflowInitContext.MessagingFactoryProxy` and `nutshell.shared.polyflow.PolyflowInitContext` ctor. The fact that compiler is not able to help you anymore will make this code more complex (because of `instanceof`-s and casts) and way more error prone.

> the only place API users have to worry about these things is in the MessagingChannels (or MessagingDefs) class.

Well, this is not true as I described above, because basically every time you would want to call `createProducer` you will have to remember what is right and what is wrong and make type checks. But more importantly you can achieve the same level of conveniency during subscribe operation just by having two overloaded methods:
```
void subscribe(TopicDef<M> topic, Consumer<M> consumer);
void subscribe(EventDef<M> event, Consumer<M> consumer);
```

And a couple of a bit less important points:
* Next, if we make a step further we will actually realize that each topic has an owner and it is not a project. So `MessagingSource.IRIS` is not enough, it is `irisflow` or `docgen` or `you_name_it` who are owners of the topics, so it should not be possible for `docgen` to publish to `irisflow_workflowevent` topic, etc
* `MessagingSource` is not enough to define a topic. Topics are not global, they belong to a project. So when we are specifying `MessageSource.GOOGLE` we also need to provide project name, and it gets even more complicated if we try to design for "cross-project messaging" now (considering CI suffixes, etc).
* `topics.yaml` will need to be converted into `messaging.yaml`, right? Which in turn increases complexity of Java/TS codegen (which we still don't have), localdev env setup (because we have to simulate eventarc in mockman, but still create topics) and terraform.

P.S.: to summarize the above, it feels to me that the proposed refactoring is much bigger than the scope of the original ticket. I also would like to have a broader discussion, because I have a strong opinion about giving up compile time safety in favor of runtime checks.

I think we've been through this before in NFS and NFT projects: pagination is hard.

From the ticket description:
> Note that [AIP 158](https://google.aip.dev/158) asks for pageSize and pageToken, where pageToken must be an opaque String. When we add pagination to our APIs, we should try to follow that, **but the DAO should just take a pageNumber.**

I would suggest we revisit the last statement. Page number/page size combo is generally a poor choice (as, to a lesser extent, is page offset / page size) for multiple reasons:
* (minor, usability) you can't adjust page size on the fly, like you can't continue where you left off and request 100 items instead of 20 items for your next page (not an issue if we use page offset/size combo)
* (minor, consistency) you have a risk of showing duplicates if you do lazy loading on the UI as you scroll and new item is added to the previous page before you requested the next one
* (major, consistency) there may be ties in the sorting. Like if you sort people by age, more than 1 person can have age of 30 years old. You have to do extra work to guarantee stable sorting, otherwise you may get the same people on page 1 and page 2 if the same age is spread across these two pages
* (major, performance) `LIMIT X OFFSET Y` is simply slow when offset is large enough, it always does linear scan of all the results from row 0 and discards Y first elements before returning you the result. So with each page your queries will become progressively slower and slower

Alternative is to use last item's ID as page token. It makes a query very simple and it makes execution super quick, and it also eliminates minor usability issues I mentioned above

I have several concerns here
(1) My general concern is that committing to have a separate proto for each custom might be an overkill. Sure if we don't grow, that doesn't matter. 
But we are here because we want Nutshell to grow, _and_ if we do, this message will quickly become HUGE without particular reason.

(2) My very specific concern is that we diluted the notion of document type even further. 

In most places in Iris we don't really care about the template per se, we care only about what document type it is (like various places in UI and in reporting job for instance), and we usually know things about "client" via configuration.

What I don't see in this proposal is how reporting job request is going to look like, and it is not an easy answer. If we mimic the same "oneof" approach the implementation and maintainability will suffer big time, because here's how the code building ES query will transform all of a sudden:
```java
if (request.isBrokerageStatement()) {
  query = """
    doc.template_input.input.oneof IN (
       "m1_brokerage_statement", 
       "apex_brokerage_statement", 
       ...<10 other customer's brokerage statements>...,
       "whatever_brokerage_statement"
    ) AND <actually_useful_part_of_a_query>
    """;
} else {
..
}
```
and we're going to do that for every single template we add. I am 100% sure that we're going to _always_ forget to update reporting job to support new client.

And in fact, it is actually even worse, because `oneof` does not get serialized into JSON and doesn't even make it into Elasticsearch. So the actual query will look even worse:
```java
if (request.isBrokerageStatement()) {
  query = """
    (doc.template_input.input.m1_brokerage_statement != null OR
    doc.template_input.input.apex_brokerage_statement != null OR
    doc.template_input.input.whatever_brokerage_statement != null OR
    ...<10 other customer's brokerage statements>...)
    AND <actually_useful_part_of_a_query>
    """;
}
```

I have a gut feeling that in many other places (like in Email service) we will have to do something similar just to understand what document type is in front of us. 
_AND_ we'll have to update all the places where it happens when we make a change.

Please note that this is unrelated to bulk client, but is an important fix which otherwise generated a massive lock contention during Spanner writes.

I accidentally introduced this bug with a last minute schema change in `no doc table` PR: I removed `deleted` field from `document_job_id_failed` index.

This was totally unnecessary as Spanner guarantees that it will only close change stream read cursor when all transactions within [from; to] interval were returned, PLUS it effectively introduced guaranteed latency of up to 1.5 seconds before we start processing data updates.

It may take up to 10-20 seconds to process an update in `DeliveryStreamProcessor`, and obviously all other processors (i.e Docjob) would wait until that happen. Moving it (temporary) out into its own thread / HWM makes it possible to make things demo-able again.

There are several reasons why we shouldn't.

First, and most important one, our Change Streams' capture type is configured to `NEW_ROW`. Read more about it here: [Value capture types](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/change-streams#value-capture-type). What it gives us is that we always get a full row of every Spanner update regardless of how many columns were changed. For instance, soft-deletes only update `deleted` column and it is super handy.
As a consequence, we don't get any data except primary key if we actually hard-delete stuff. I hard-deleted a buggy workflow from dev-kb yesterday when I was testing Job Copy, and you can see the data change record shape [here](https://console.cloud.google.com/logs/query;query=resource.type%20%3D%20%22cloud_run_revision%22%0Aresource.labels.service_name%20%3D%20%22cdc-kb%22%0Aresource.labels.location%20%3D%20%22us-central1%22%0A%20severity%3E%3DERROR;pinnedLogId=2024-03-11T13:31:32.600Z%2F1lpreqnf7oa1ig;cursorTimestamp=2024-03-11T13:31:34.313Z;aroundTime=2024-03-11T13:31:32.600Z;duration=PT1H?project=prj-d-iris-kb-z5t3&rapt=AEjHL4OZceniYT6grHDiJJOrcCFCSb656t7e6VFvMX-D7bDGJT5NAp_W1DnmawFFL110Uf24sqgSo-b7MumdJoo6euqgVVk1d-VKZ1TiqEnQQ9v1MFB5A6E).

Second reason in my opinion is also quite important: don't write code which you don't need. Because not only that you need to cover it with tests and maintain when you do refactors and stuff, you also give an impression that it is a normal execution path and deletes are normal. And they are not.

Finally, if CDC ever sees deleted stuff, it either happened due to a bug, or intentionally due to some manual intervention.
* if it happened due to a bug, I'd prefer not to cover this bug with some code and pretend that everything is fine, but rather signal that there _is_ a bug which causes deletes, hence the logs (ideally we should have alerting set up to notify us when that happens)
* and if it happened manually, then it is not a big deal to go and send a delete query to ES also (I literally did that yesterday in dev-kb when I found a bug in my workflow, see logs above)

This is the example of how CEL expression makes it possible to transform root's `JobInput` proto into something else, in this case it is `LongRunninOperationRequest`.

Syntax is very close to `golang`'s syntax:
```go
fully.qualified.proto.Name {
   field1: value1,
   field2: value2,
...
   fieldN: valueN
}
```

In this particular example I create a long running operation request with `document_job_report_request` (which is `oneof`) set to `node_output.job_id` where `node_output` is root node's output (i.e `JobInput`) proto

Now, as I said a billion times over the course of last 12 months or so: how we do demo jobs is not how we potentially want to do real jobs. 1. Views in Spanner are just queries, so their only benefit is readability. For example, in this particular query I could've converted all CTEs into a view `DocsWithUnsentDeliveries`, and then in the end just
```sql
SELECT
    document.*
FROM
    document JOIN DocsWithUnsentDeliveries
ON
    document.id = DocsWithUnsentDeliveries.document_id
```
2. The problem with this approach though is that in order to understand what's happening you'll need to look at both `schema.sql` and here, which in my opinion makes it less readable.
3. Counting delivery configs are not enough. We need to track each email (and phone number, but we don't care about those for now) in each delivery config separately. That's exactly what `FlattenedDeliveries` CTE is: it produces 1 row per each email and each phone number in all delivery configs per document.
4. Finally, what's happening here is almost exactly what you propose, but instead of counting, `FlattenedDelivery` gets `LEFT JOIN`-ed to delivery table and the ones that don't have delivery get picked.

Essentially, this is exactly the same query as it was before, but instead of `document LEFT JOIN delivery` we do `FlattenedDeliveries LEFT JOIN delivery`. And we get `FlattenedDeliveries` by first `UNNEST`-ing an array of all delivery configs per document, producing `D` rows as a result per document, where `D` is delivery config count, and then we also `UNNEST`-ing array of emails (`repeated string email`), and producing `D * E` rows per document where `E` is number of emails in each delivery config.

So for example, if you have 2 delivery configs, one with 1 email and another with 2 emails in document `foo`, you'll end up with 3 rows for doc `foo` in `FlattenedDeliveries`.

A couple of notes and nitpicks here:
* `mapWorkflowNodes` can not be empty, as workflows without nodes don't exist (and our builders and code in other places doesn't allow it),
* even if we pretend that this is possible, this algorithm is confusing, because it produces two different outcomes for basically the same use case: `protoRef` has less number of nodes than `getDag()`, then
    * if `protoRef` is empty, i.e. during workflow augmentation, we deleted all the nodes, then... suddenly workflow remains the same and ignores our actions
    * if `protoRef` has just one (or more, but not all) nodes deleted, then those nodes loose all their parents, which again produces incorrect DAG from polyflow standpoint (we will have more than 1 root)

In other words, what I am saying here is that generally we need to be careful with "defensive programming", which lines 99 and 107 in the above block of code represent:
* you're trying to protect your algorithm from failing / throwing an exception when the input is incorrect, which is a noble intention, however...
* you end up with a corrupt / incorrect state from the logical standpoint which 
    * is probably going to cause the code elsewhere to fail later, 
    * or, even worse, will mask a bug which will be hard to detect and investigate because we saw no failures, but ended up with a broken DAG which polyflow can't process properly.

This was a very long way to say:
* if your code detects a condition that shouldn't happen (both if `protoRef` has 0 nodes or has less nodes that the original workflow), it _must_ fail and _must not_ hide the fact that something went wrong.

So if we look at the problem from this new angle, forgetting about `iris`, `aria`, etc for a second, polyflow is very straightforward as a lib:
* it always have full workflow loaded into memory
* it executes nodes one by one, sequentially and synchronously.

In other words, when you call `workflow.execute()`, your thread is blocked, not even blocked but your thread _is_ the thread that is doing the work, so the execution is always synchronous. Since we now recognize that, the concept of async execution, i.e in calling `workflow.execute()` and having _somebody else_ to actually do the job, makes sense right? 

(I am not saying here btw that the abstractions that I introduced here are sane, that's something I am not confident about, but I think the concept of "async execution of a polyflow workflow" totally makes sense from the library standpoint.)

In my view, polyflow should be abstract enough to not care what async execution means: 
* it may also literally mean "execute in that ScheduledExecutor" or something, if we're not in GCP but in pure Kubernetes like we were with NFTs,
* "execute asynchronously in GCP/AWS" may also mean different things, like you may want to send a pub/sub message to a worker service

but it provides a "plug-n-play" framework to enable that behavior: create a subclass of `AsyncExecutionPlugin` and fill in the gaps.

> Is this true?

Yes, nodes are _expected_ to be idempotent. There is no "exactly one run" guarantee in polyflow.

> Any workflow could be rerun from the start and there would be no change of external state?

I don't think that the statement `the whole workflow is idempotent` is equivalent to `each node is idempotent`. 

Indeed, in an M1 docjob:
* you can execute and then re-execute M1 data collector (pre-ingest node) and you'll get the same result. 
* after it's done, you can execute and then re-execute ingest and you will produce an equivalent result, even though it is not byte-by-byte equal. 
* after that, you can safely re-run docgen job even 100 times and it will not duplicate documents,
* same with warnings policies, they're already in place, etc. 

But if you rollback the whole thing, there will be dupes because Ingest produces non-deterministic UUIDs for their outputs. It is quite easy to fix to be honest, but it is a way stronger requirement than "at any given time an ACTIVE node may execute twice without causing additional side-effects" and we're not pursuing that.

> I like ietf's definitions for this type of specification. https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt I suspect this is a "SHOULD" not a "MUST" or "MAY".

Honestly, I think that's a `MUST`. For example, we're using marketing campaign ID in deliveries exactly because of this `MUST`. 

But the reality is that not all workflows made equal. I literally don't care if doc story workflow and / or any of its nodes are idempotent, even though I still expect it to be so.

> Is ingest idempotent then? Seems like it isn't (which totally makes sense).

It is. It has several mechanisms to provide that property:
* first, it produces a stable job name, so that even in case of some PubSub double-delivery, for example, it will make 2 requests to Dataflow, but the second one returns 409.
* then, even if it happens (and that actually did happened in M1 prod, when we produced our very first Aug statements, and I still don't know what the root cause was), that after completion of one ingest job another one is requested immediately, because the job itself produces stable output file names, it will overwrite the output of the first job and everything downstream will work correctly.

As I said, statement "Node is idempotent" is not equivalent to "Workflow is idempotent".

Here's the simplified example of a workflow, where each node itself is idempotent, but the whole thing is definitely not:
* `root` node receives an input with a number N
* Node `A` produces N files with stable filenames "1.txt", "2.txt", ... "N.txt", and puts it into a bucket `work-queue`. After that Node `A` succeeds.
* Then for each file in `work-queue`, Node `B` reads its metadata, then deletes it, and if delete is successful, Node `B` writes the file creation timestamp from that metadata to the Spanner table `event`.

`A` is easily idempotent: it may even not check if file `X.txt` exists prior to writing, it doesn't matter. But let's imagine it does check it, so it produces literally 0 side effects if it runs concurrently in two different threads.
`B` is also idempotent, because even if triggered twice from two different threads after `A` completes, it will still only delete N files and will write only N events, because if things happen concurrently only 1 delete operation succeeds per file.

However, once the workflow is done, if you start it over, you'll end up with twice as many events in your `event` table. 

I can even give you a sillier example: Node A writes something with stable IDs based on workflow own ID to Spanner, then Node B drops the database. 😄 If you rerun everything Node A will crash because DB doesn't exist, and workflow will fail.

By the way, it is very easy to make any workflow "workflow-level-idempotent". How? Polyflow can check if there is a record in `workflow_history` table with this workflow's ID and status `SUCCESS`. If yes, just mark all the nodes as successful and quit 😆 This is silly, and this is not our goal.

By requiring idempotency here, we're not asking that "any node can be re-run at any time, even 100 days later, and everything should be fine", we're asking:
"Look, due to the nature of polyflow, it may happen that _this node_'s execution will happen twice because:
* two different threads / processes can easily start executing it simultaneously,
* or an unexpected exception will be thrown in the middle of execution and PubSub will redeliver the message in 5 secs
* or something along those lines

so please make sure you don't duplicate / multiply things if that happens."

Strictly speaking, `volatile` has nothing to do with double-check locking. `volatile` tells threads not to cache variable values in their internal cache. That's it. In other words every time the variable is accessed it needs to be read from the memory. 

`volatile`, however, is required for double-check locking to work correctly, because without it you have a good chance of already non-null variable being read as `null` by _this_ thread because it was cached in the thread's internals.

Purely from the compliance perspective, this raises a big question if such an action is legitimate:
* first, by hard-deleting a client you basically remove all the traces about it without leaving a chance to refer back to the data that was there before:
    * you can no longer `JOIN` some tables with client-info / big config in order to figure out what config was used at what point in time, etc
* then, by allowing the creation of the "new" client with once-existing ID you generate even more confusion: is it the same company? is it the same legal entity? is it responsible for all the docs that were created a year ago with the same client ID? what if I accidentally join this "new" client with old data that has the same client ID?
* also, this messes up with an upcoming feature work on client-level permissions MASSIVELY,
* finally, we have other mechanisms of preserving the history if we wanted to, like `_history` tables, etc

TL;DR we should NOT allow that. IDs should be unique. Once assigned, they should never be unassigned. They should never be changed (and Spanner doesn't allow this to happen for a reason). All the deletes should be "soft-deletes".

So I think what should happen is, in transaction:
* you mark all the big configs for this client as `STATUS_ARCHIVED`
* you soft-delete a row from `client_info`, this should be a terminal operation and new client with the same ID should not be allowed

* an app that we deploy
* a gRPC service in protobufs
* a guy who initializes the connection to spanner -- SpannerService.java, (and others like that)
* a guy who implements a gRPC service

At times, it was too confusing for AI to understand which service is being referred in the prompt. The situation worsened by the naming of one of our gRPC services: `IrisflowService`. So for Java, the decision was to rename everything except gRPC services, because unfortunately that's the part of the protobuf defintion language, we can't take it out:

```protobuf
service IrisService {
  /* Internal API for Aether UI */
  rpc CreateJob(CreateJobRequest) returns (CreateJobResponse);
<...>
```

The golden rule of Integration and End-to-end tests: they should never depend on the service's code.

The reason behind this is that integration tests verify among other things the API contracts that were established. Workflow definition ID is the part of the API, changing it in the service code will lead to widespread problems elsewhere even though all the unit-tests will pass because they rely on the compiled code. If you changed the compiled code, unit-test would naturally just use that new compiled code and everything will match / pass.

In integration tests, it is _extremely_ important that we always use string literals in the places like this, so whenever somebody (either intentionally or by accident) changes the workflow definition ID (e.g by moving it to another package without overriding `id()` method), this integration test will catch that and we all will be thankful.

So (a) please remove the dependencies that you've added to the integration test and (b) use string literal here as the worklfow defintion id

P.S.: this also applies to workflow node labels, that's why if you look around you'll see that everywhere in Int/E2E tests we always use constructions like
```
waitForNodeCompletion(workflow, "apply-smp");
```
and never
```
waitForNodeCompletion(workflow, DocJobWorkflowDef.APPLY_SMP_NODE);
```

Great question. I think it's not an easy one.

In order to answer this question, we should first ask ourselves, what does this function actually do?
To me, the right answer to that question is
* it makes sure that we get the right documents from ES according to the provided request.

Note that I didn't say "it construct elasticsearch request of a certain shape". There's potentially infinite amount of ES requests that produce exactly the same result, right? So are we interested in the request or in the result?

In my opinion, once again, I am interested in the result. Which means that the ultimate unit-test that I want to have is:
* by sending certain API request (not ES request!) I want to be sure that I get _certain_ documents back as a result

That's why this function is not being tested _directly_, it is being tested indirectly: see `documents_test.go` (I've added a lot more test-cases to `TestSearchDocuments` to reinforce my point here, so thank you for raising concerns!!!)

Another benefit that such an approach brings is that I am now free to refactor the code and rewrite the ES query if I find some more optimized or elegant way of querying the same stuff, without updating any tests, more than that, existing tests _ensure_ that if I make a mistake in my refactor, it'll be caught. Whereas if I only had a unit-test that verified certain ES query shape, I wouldn't be able to verify if my new code actually works the same way as previous code.

TL;DR:
* unit-tests that you proposed are _WAY BETTER_ than having no tests at all, don't get me wrong
* however, I think there's a step forward that you can make to improve upon that approach and have our business expectations validated instead
* which in turn liberates us in terms of refactoring later down the road

P.S.: there's still value in having pure unit-tests that check that we produce certain shape of an ES query, but that is not necessarily about the filters. It may be some technical detail, like do we provide a correct "preference" string (the "preference" string in ES query parameters ensures that we hit exactly the same shard every time, so that our results are stable). There's no way to validate that we provide the right preference string just by looking at the ES query results in our unit-tests in `documents_test.go`, so the only option to ensure that is to have the unit-test of `buildDocumentsSearchQuery`

P.P.S: but that raises a new question, are we 100% confident that `buildDocumentsSearchQuery` is called every time we call SearchDocuments endpoint? 😉

RE: zod (and ts-match). I'll reply here as Github doesn't allow to reply to non-line-based PR comments.

Zod is a useful lib but I think it's practical use-case is different and way more narrow then we used to think. I can give you a simple example of what I mean and why `something.field ?? ""` is better than Zod.

Let's imagine we have a bug in Bff or Backend or CDC, or whatever, and some API call that usually returns
```
{ id: "foo", name: "bar" }
```
that is by contract guaranteed to return both fields as non-empty strings, suddenly omits name. Just a bug.

Now if we have a Zod schema that enforces that validation at the response time, we'll get an error screen, right? Stuff doesn't work, we have display error page 500 or whatever. So what happens is that we prevent the rest of the screen / UI from working, even though this could be just a tiny secondary element in a table that we don't really care much about.

We already have a bug, we know it, but instead of limiting the impact by just filling the affected field on the UI as empty string or `<missing>` placeholder or something, we crash. This I never liked and understood about Zod. Yeah it does make it somewhat easier to develop stuff and it makes it kind of a bit clearer what exactly goes wrong, but it is terrible in production. In production, most of the time, we want too carry on regardless of the bad data coming from BE, but with Zod, we can't.

Now finally, and I think even more importantly `something.field ?? ""` is an absolute piece of cake for AI. It doesn't get tired by doing that everywhere, trust me. Humans would've hated that, but we shouldn't force humans to write FE. AI is much better at it and much faster.

Same applies to ts-match. Yes, ts-match is neat and powerful, providing you care about your types. But AI usually doesn't care about clean types and AI doesn't use it even though it's a dependency in the library. So why enforce that if practical result is absolutely the same, but using ts-match is just more burdensome for both you and AI, because AI will never use it free-willingly and you, as an AI user, will always waste time asking AI to correct that.

This is a (potentially! see my P.S. notes below) breaking change currently as it is, but it's an easy one to fix.

Currently, as it stands, we have two types of jobs in Spanner:
* older ones, that only had one (now deprecated) `document_type` field set in their root node's output
* newer ones, that only set `repeated document_types` in their root node output.

When new multi-doc-type jobs were introduced, there was also a change made to the CDC to ensure backwards compatibility with Aether: CDC retrofits `job.root.output.document_types[0]` into `job.root.output.document_type` when the latter is empty.

So far so good, right?

With this change, however, you added a new `document_types` field to the BFF API and updated the FE to use it which is great, that's what we want. 

However, there are still older jobs that never had `document_types` array set. Therefore if you open any of the older jobs in aether using this code, it won't see any document types set at all (because FE doesn't read singular old `document_type` field anymore).

What should happen here is
* singular `string document_type` should be removed / converted into `repeated string document_types` (we don't have to keep BFF APIs backwards compatible because they ship together with aether) -- **UPD: see my new comment below on that**
* here, on the BFF side, you should account for the potential older jobs that have only singular `document_type` set, in a following way:
```go
// pseudo-code, Golang doesn't have ternary operator
DocumentTypes: len(root.DocumentTypes) == 0 ? [root.DocumentType] : root.DocumentTypes,
```

This way you ensure full "forward-compatibility" with any state you may find your ES index in.

P.S.: note that this kind of "forward-compatbility" is actually ensured on CDC level too (see go/nut/iris/cdc/document_jobs.go:272), however, we can only rely on that if we are 100% confident that we did a full index reset on Docjob2 indexes, which generally speaking you never know, so it is always a good idea to make your code robust without relying on that. 

For example, we for sure did index resets when we migrated to serverless elasticsearch, but M1 prod is still on a managed ES instance and I don't know when we did our stream reset there for the last time. 

TL;DR: to reduce headaches from thinking about all of that, it's always easier to just make your code robust and prepared for any outcome

I am not a huge fan of push-backs but I have to do it here. There are a couple of reasons why:

### Too many unrelated things in one PR

To me, this PR looks like a couple of different things squashed together (even literally in a single commit!):
1. There are changes to the PnL statement that seem reasonable to me and which I want to merge, but I can not, because
2. There are changes to how we produce outputs in an artifact template feature, which I actively worked on and had a clear vision on how to implement this, and this implementation doesn't match the design that I already have in my head.

### Why your proposed approach won't work

I'll try to lay out things from the most objective to the most opinionated (and opinionated doesn't mean those are not valid):
1. You're misinterpreting what `DocumentsManifestNode` is doing. It is not an arbitrary / internal manifest format, this manifest needs to be readable by GCS Storage Transfer Jobs and in the form that you've converted it, it won't. 
    The problem here is that mockman's `LocalDevMockStorageTransfer` is a no-op so we can't see if provided manifest is broken. I knew this will backfire when it was first introduced a year ago but I didn't push back to have a proper implementation back then. 
    And secondly, we don't have a separate integration test that tests artifact delivery to gs:// destination, because it is exactly the same nodes (until you introduced this metadata thing) that retention job uses, therefore there's no need to test them twice.
2. `ProtobufTemplate` is an unused dead-code that we should've just deleted long time ago, but didn't for some reason. The only "template engine" that we use and should use going forward is CEL expressions. CEL can do everything that this template thing can, and way more. There's no reason to introduce anything new alongside CEL.
    Admittedly, CEL is harder to write for humans, but who said humans should write it? We can build any UI that we want that will help us build any CEL expression we want with a simple, wizard/builder like UX and "pro mode" to manually edit CEL if we want to.
3. The directory structure for Artifact Delivery and the PDF output structure of the Document Generator Job is two completely different things that should have their own, independent configuration. 
    We want and can make them play nicely with one another, but there can be so many different use-cases: like one document type is only delivered to S3 bucket, but another document type for the same tenant is print-only, and the layout we may want can be wildly different. 
    It's hard to foresee what we'll need, as usual, but more flexibility upfront is almost always a better approach than jamming things into the same global config. 
    Another thing that usually works well is that "if we can get away with hardcoding something today, we should leave it hardcoded". Because tomorrow you won't need to solve a data migration problem. Output document paths are hardcoded in DocGen job now. Does it work? Yes. Does it solve today's problem? Yes. Do we want to change it tomorrow? Maybe. Do we know _what problem_ are we going to solve tomorrow? No. See? This means we shouldn't do it, if we don't know what we're doing.
4. `DocumentsManifestNode` again. Even if we assume there's no issue with GCS, I can tell it's just two different nodes squashed into a single node. Generally speaking, you have two modes: one "legacy" and one "with metadata" that are _wildly_ different from one another. If that is the case, we should always just introduce a new node type, _especially_ when you see that `DocumentManifestNode` is reused in different workflows. You did see it, right? 😉 
    And then workflow def can decide which node to use based on `hasPathTemplate` in the workflow's input with 
    ```
    .thenOnlyIf(hasPathTemplate, new NodeBuilder(NewShinyKaisNode.class))
    .thenOnlyIf(!hasPathTemplate, new NodeBuilder(LegacyManifestNode.class))
    ```

First, current open API gen is not "artisanal", well I guess if you can consider [OpenAPI Generator](https://github.com/OpenAPITools/openapi-generator) project with 26k stars, 7.5k forks and over 13k closed PRs aritsanal, then I won't object 😄 

The only "artisanal" part in it that I added on top is exactly because of this (see highlighted lines 7-10): I wanted to avoid having fully-qualified names in the codebase, because it's harder to read and quite ugly:
* I extended the vanilla typescript fetch generator from OpenAPI Gen and made it "package aware" (see `PackageAwareTsFetchCodegen`), in other words I made it so that it properly sorts the `nutshell.iris.foo.Bar` proto into `nutshell/iris/foo/Bar.ts` file as opposed to having it like this `NutshellIrisFooBar`
* then I added a post-processing script that just puts `index.ts` files in all those subpackages because it was easier to do so as a post-processing step instead of hacking OpenAPI generator further

If we remove both of those things, we'll get exactly the same result with 0 artisanal parts, but as I said, I think it's quite valuable to get rid of those FQN even though I know it can be solved at the import time:
```
import type {
  NutshellIrisProtoAetherSystemGetAuthStatusResponse as GetStatusResponse,
  NutshellIrisProtoAetherSystemLogoutResponse as LogoutResponse,
} from "@/orval/gen/model";
```

The problem with ⬆️ is that it WILL generate friction with LLMs. LLMs will constantly "forget" to do so and will just import FQN because they don't give a shit. But we, humans, do, and I think it's important to have nice(er)-to-read codebase.

P.S.: it's funny that I actually implemented this "artisanal" part on top just like a crowd-pleaser basically, because I thought that if I showed the shiny-new approach with ugly looking APIs, it will immediately be perceived as a "regression" compared to what we had with proto-ts, but turns out it doesn't bother anyone 

P.P.S: I still kind of believe that API object names that 100% match proto message names are of a great value (for both humans, and AI actually).

[2] is not so much about authentication (we shouldn't have any in Docgen), but about the pattern of putting a Http-to-gRPC gateway as a standalone app (in case of localdev) or as a sidecar container (in case of the deployment to cloud run) in front of any service that serves pure gRPC without making the service in question be responsible for that.

We have a purely local situation here:
1. Devtool runs on pure Vite devserver (aka it's backend-less), it's awesome because:
   * we can think of docgen itself as a backend for devtool
   * but we don't want to "teach" docgen to speak HTTP, because it's not docgen's concern
   * we don't want to introduce a new backend and TS/Go app (as it uses bazel build time, even though not too much, but still), while we don't really need it anywhere except localdev
2. What we want, and can do, instead is to start a new `grpc-gateway` process in Tiltfile and just connect to it as Docgen-proxy
    * that one we need to generalize first, to accept any gRPC service as it currently only accepts public API, 
    * currently it is hardcoded in `gateway_nut.go` (yep, we have two different `gateway_nut.go`, we probably should rename them into `embedded_` and `standalone_` or something)
    * I am thinking we can even codegen the `go/app/iris/grpc_gateway/main.go` and have a lightweight bazel macro that takes gRPC service dependency and the name of the service, and then codgens the rest and produces grpc_gateway binaries that can serve various gRPCs

There are downsides to [2] too JFYI:
* we need to annotate docgen API with HTTP annotations that we don't _really_ need
* we need to make aforementioned code changes to grpc_gateway to make it generic

So the lesson here is that there are no rights and wrongs most of the time, it's just about thinking about all the options and picking your trade offs.

I don't think you got the idea right. 

What I want to remove is fragile situation we're currently in:
* we receive data in `M` tables and convert it basically into `N` new tables (CSV files) using BigQuery
* we start ingest job and "join" these `N` tables into `K` documents

Issues with this are:
* this `M -> N` conversion is done by N independent queries (yes, they share some CTEs but still independent), the probability that you grab extra data or miss some data is quite high
* this `N -> K` conversion is done by a huge chunk of handwritten CSV parsing java-code that on its own is tedious to support and can lead to errors

I don't want to move anything to Cloud Run Job, I want to use the same approach as in tax: 
* BQ is capable of producing "raw" input that just does `M -> K` right away 

So I just want BQ to produce something similar to what we now call `CoinTrackerInput`, which:
* has a clearly expressed type as protobuf, i.e `M1BrokerageStatementInput`, `M1CreditCardStatementInput`, etc
* that needs just a simple 1-1 transformation in Ingest, similarly to `CoinTrackerMapper`, we can have a simple class `M1BrokerageStatementMapper` that basically does the same thing we now do in `Combine` PTransforms.

The benefits are obvious:
* we run 1 BQ query instead of `N` queries per data collector run, which 
    * will be less error-prone and much faster overall (i.e will spend less compute, as you only need to run `eiligible_accounts` CTE once)
    * make the data collector itself quite tiny and simple
* we produce exactly K documents that we need right away, simplifying ingest job dramatically by removing a huge layer of CSV-to-proto transformation

That's not how `IngestJob` works. 

It's possible to read from multiple arbitrarily located sources in Apache Beam, that's obviously true, but `IngestJob` currently reads only 1 input file pattern and then passes data into reader.

So you either:
* in `PreIngestNode`, grab all the JSONs you want and ZIP them and drop into a known location (like `iris-input` bucket that we have)
* or just provide `gs://pre-ingest/parittion-date=blah/job=1/*.json` (note the asterisk)

Then `AtomicManifestReader` needs to learn how to distinguish rows from one file from rows from another file, because those are just JSONs, it's not super trivial.

So my recommendation would be to
* create protobufs that match those JSONs in `dataflow.proto`
* in PreIngest read both files, parse each row as corresponding protobufs (in strict mode, so it fails if it encounters unknown fields)
* serialize them as `Any` JSON and write to the output location in `iris-input` bucket, possibly even into the same file
* this file (or set of files with `*.jsonl` pattern) becomes an input for `IngestJob`

Then later in `AtomicManifestReader` each row is deserialized from JSON into `Any` and then the logic is based on the type.

**ALTERNATIVELY**, you can just pass a `gs://<input>/*.json` pattern directly and rely on the `nutshell.shared.dataflow.job.Source` that accompanies every row that is returned to figure out, to which file the string row belongs to. I would say this is easier to start with, but maybe a bit more fragile? Not sure. Maybe not. You have to rely on "hardcoded" filenames in both cases.

So I think we probably should start with `Source` inspection and later add complexity to PreIngestNode if we feel like it's helpful.

We should always use request-response node pattern because of the concurrent nature of events. If single node sends a request that is immediately processed and receives a pub-sub response before the workflow state was saved, the message won't be processed and will be lost.

Dataflow batch nodes break this pattern, true, but this is because (a) historical reasons (it was created super long time ago before workflow augmentation existed, so it manages complicated stuff like automatic retries, handling of 409s, etc)
and (b) we know dataflow is quite slow in practice so the chance that we receive an update before we saved the state is low. 

Also, even if that happens, the update that we'll miss is going to be like `STATE_CREATED` and that is not a big deal.

So TL;DR always use request-response pattern AND always put response node first (so it activates before we send any requests)

Sharding here is introduced mostly to support basically unlimited scale.
When you're running scanner query like "hey find me all the forms that I haven't submitted yet" on a test database, you're fine, you can grab literally all of those forms from a single query and process them 1 by 1 using `consume` function (important not to read the whole thing into memory still, even if DB is small).

message WorkflowData {

* internal fields that are needed by bump library
* `google.protobuf.Any payload = X` with something that control plane needs

rpc InitializeRequest(...) returns (BumpPreHandle); // pre handle is not exposed to the user space

message BumpHandleDescriptor {
    BumpPreHandle pre_handle = 1; // all that Bump lib needs
    google.protobuf.Any payload = 2; // all that Control Plane needs

The more I think about it the more I am convinced that just pure hashing of the proto above is not the right solution.

We're not doing anything here, but for the future work related to it:
* per each model we should have a distinct separate `HashCalculator`
* this hash calculator should establish an explicit hashing algorithm that calculates it against the established explicit order of the fields in the proto
* not all fields, in principle, should participate in hashing 

Example: we have `string date_of_birth = X;` which we want to replace with `DateOfBirht date_of_birth = Y;` which has 3 separate fields: day, month, year. 

Data hasn't changed. We still have date of birth there, but the proto shape did. So we should be able to calculate totally new snapshot without any version increments. This will allow us to evolve protobuf models without triggering version updates. Without this mechanism in place, the future will be painful.

Another example: we have `Instrument` model for brokerage and the only thing that has changed is that we added `description`. Should we regenerate PDFs? Maybe, but most likely we should not. So we need a tool to make that decision. Brute-force hashing deprives us from that.
